exercises.objective: Verify a candidate matrix is a valid rotation matrix.
exercises.prompt: Verify that $R=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$ (a 90° rotation about the $z$-axis) satisfies both $SO(3)$ conditions. Then explain why $R'=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ (same first two rows, but flipped sign in the bottom-right) is *not* a valid rotation matrix, even though its columns are still orthonormal.
hints: Compute $R^\top R$ directly (or note that the columns of $R$ are visibly unit length and mutually orthogonal, e.g. $(0,1,0)\cdot(-1,0,0)=0$), confirming $R^\top R=I$.
Compute $\det(R)$ (e.g. by cofactor expansion along the third row, which has only one nonzero entry): $\det(R) = 1\times\det\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} = 1\times(0-(-1)) = 1$.

For $R'$: its columns are still orthonormal (the sign flip in one entry doesn't break orthogonality or unit length), so $R'^\top R'=I$ still holds, but $\det(R') = -1$ (the sign flip negates the determinant). $R'$ is an orthonormal matrix but a **reflection**, not a rotation, exactly why $SO(3)$ requires both conditions, orthonormality alone isn't enough to rule out reflections.

exercises.objective: Apply Rodrigues' formula to rotate a vector by hand.
exercises.prompt: Using Rodrigues' formula, rotate $v=(1,0,0)$ by $\theta=\pi/3$ (60°) about axis $\hat w=(0,0,1)$. Report the **second component** ($y$) of the result. Enter a decimal to 3 decimal places.
hints: $\hat w\times v = (0,0,1)\times(1,0,0) = (0,1,0)$ (standard cross product), and $\hat w^\top v = 0$ (they're perpendicular), so the third term of Rodrigues' formula vanishes entirely here.
Rodrigues' formula reduces to $\cos\theta\,v+\sin\theta\,(\hat w\times v) = \cos(\pi/3)(1,0,0)+\sin(\pi/3)(0,1,0)$.

exercises.objective: Derive the rotation-matrix angular-velocity identity from the geometric definition of angular velocity.

sourceRef.originalNumber: Angular velocity & derivative of a rotation matrix

exercises.prompt: Let $x_{\text{body}}$ be a point fixed in a body rotating with angular velocity $w$, so its world position is $x(t)=R(t)x_{\text{body}}$. The geometric definition of angular velocity says $\dot x(t) = w\times x(t)$ (a point rotating rigidly about the origin has velocity equal to $w\times$ its current position). Using this, and that $x_{\text{body}}$ is an *arbitrary* fixed body point, derive $\dot R(t)=\text{skew}(w)R(t)$.
hints: Differentiate $x(t)=R(t)x_{\text{body}}$ directly: $\dot x(t) = \dot R(t)x_{\text{body}}$ (since $x_{\text{body}}$ is constant).
Also, by the geometric definition, $\dot x(t) = w\times x(t) = \text{skew}(w)x(t) = \text{skew}(w)R(t)x_{\text{body}}$ (using $\text{skew}(w)v=w\times v$ and substituting $x(t)=R(t)x_{\text{body}}$).

Both expressions equal $\dot x(t)$, so $\dot R(t)x_{\text{body}} = \text{skew}(w)R(t)x_{\text{body}}$. Since this holds for *every* choice of fixed body point $x_{\text{body}}\in\mathbb{R}^3$ (not just one specific one), the matrices multiplying $x_{\text{body}}$ on each side must themselves be equal: $\dot R(t)=\text{skew}(w)R(t)$.

exercises.objective: Compose two homogeneous transforms and convert a point's coordinates through both frames.
exercises.prompt: World frame $W$, frame $A$: $R_{W\to A}=I$, $t_{W\to A}=(2,0,0)$. Frame $B$ relative to $A$: $R_{A\to B}$ is a 90° rotation about $z$ (as in the first exercise), $t_{A\to B}=(0,1,0)$. A point has coordinates $x^B=(1,0,0)$ in frame $B$. Compute $x^W$ (first convert $x^B\to x^A$, then $x^A\to x^W$), and report the **second component** ($y$). Enter a decimal.
